## Method

- **Burst:** 10,000 readings from 200 sensors × 3 types (temperature, humidity, co2), generated up front and dispatched at once by the project's simulator (`runBurst`, undici keep-alive pool). The client runs on the same machine as the server and the database.
- **Rules:** 24 enabled rules (THRESHOLD and WINDOW, per `loadtest/seed-rules.ts`), some of which fire on normal data, so rule evaluation and alert upserts are part of the measured cost.
- **Server:** production build (`dist/server.js`), request logging off, against a freshly migrated dedicated database. A warm-up burst (excluded) runs first.
- **Runs:** 3 per scenario, 1 s apart.
- **Completion time:** from the first request to the last response. Every `202` is sent only after the reading is committed, so this is also time-to-persisted.
- **Latency:** per HTTP request, from send to full response.
- **Server usage:** measured inside the server by a probe preloaded only for the load test (`loadtest/probe.mjs`, reporting over IPC, so sampling launches no processes). CPU = CPU time ÷ wall time (100% = one core); event-loop busy = share of the burst the JavaScript thread was working; RSS = peak resident memory.
- **DB check:** rows added to `readings` during the run must equal readings accepted.

## Analysis

### Headline

In the recorded run above, all three burst shapes pass. Further validation runs show:
- **Batches** pass with a wide margin every time.
- **Single-reading bursts (LT-C)** pass in most runs but not all on this 15 W laptop (see *Repeatability* below).

In every run of every scenario there were zero failed requests, and the database row count matched the accepted count exactly (FR-3.1). Durability was never relaxed: `synchronous_commit` stays `on`, and every `202` waits for the commit.

| Shape | Completion seen | Throughput | Margin against the 3 s limit (FR-3.2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Batches (LT-A, LT-B) | 0.14–0.44 s in every probe-measured run with default settings | ~20–70k readings/s | ≥ 5×, every run |
| Single readings (LT-C, 512 connections) | 0.81–3.39 s | ~3–12k requests/s | ~1–3×; see below |

### Repeatability of LT-C

After the recorded run, LT-C was repeated 11 more times: once from a fresh clone, then 2 × 5 runs. Runs with the CPU profiler attached are excluded.

| Validation runs | Completion | Missed p99 < 2 s (NFR-2) | Missed completion < 3 s (FR-3.2) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | 1.56–3.39 s (median 2.07 s) | 5 | 2 (both were the first run after warm-up) |

- **FR-3.1 always held:** 0 failed requests, all 10,000 readings stored, every run.
- **The completion and latency targets** were met in the recorded run, but in only 6 of 11 validation runs for p99, and in 9 of 11 for the 3 s limit.
- **Why it varies:** the same work takes more CPU time in slow runs (event loop typically 70–86% busy, versus 61–71% in the recorded run). This matches a hybrid laptop CPU (2 performance + 10 efficiency cores, 15 W) whose effective speed depends on which core the server thread lands on and on boost and thermal state.
- **Why it is close to the limit at all:** a CPU profile of the server under LT-C (`LOADTEST_SERVER_NODE_ARGS="--cpu-prof"`) attributes **~36% of busy CPU time to `writev`**, the system call that writes each HTTP response to its socket (Fastify → `http` → `net`). Other contributions:
  - application code (rule evaluation, sliding windows, validation): ~9%;
  - the PostgreSQL driver: ~5%;
  - Fastify: ~4%;
  - GC: ~4%.

  One socket write per response is inherent to single-reading requests, and on this Windows machine it is expensive. No application change removes it. What would:
  - **batching**, the same 10,000 readings in ≥ 100-reading batches: ≥ 5× margin in every run;
  - a **Linux** host, where socket writes are much cheaper;
  - **more HTTP processes** in front of a single window owner (scale-out path in [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md)).

### Where the time goes

1. **Single requests are limited by per-request work on one event loop.** In LT-C the JavaScript thread is 61–71% busy for the whole burst. That's roughly 60–100 µs per request for HTTP parsing, routing, validation and the reply on this CPU. Batching amortises this cost over up to 1,000 readings, which is why LT-A and LT-B are about 5× faster with the event loop only 39–56% busy.
2. **Reply-after-commit bounds what one connection can push.** Each request waits for the next group commit: up to `FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS` in the queue plus one commit, about 30–40 ms. A client connection sends one request at a time. So single-reading throughput is roughly connections ÷ 35 ms until the event loop saturates (sweep below). This latency is the price of the no-loss guarantee (design §9).
3. **Batches are limited by PostgreSQL commits and hot alert rows.** Inserting 2,000 rows takes about 15–40 ms. During a burst, most batches update the same few hundred active alerts (`triggerCount`, about 5,300 triggers per burst here). Sampling `pg_stat_activity` showed overlapping transactions waiting on `Lock:transactionid` in the alert upsert. Overlap still pays off: while one transaction waits on a lock, another inserts readings (flush sweep below).

### Tuning experiments

These are separate exploratory runs of `pnpm loadtest --no-report`, 3 runs each, values are medians. The defaults were kept because they performed best.

**Flush settings, batch scenarios (completion ms):**

| `FLUSH_CONCURRENCY` | `FLUSH_MAX_ROWS` | `FLUSH_INTERVAL_MS` | LT-A | LT-B |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **3** | **2000** | **10** (default) | **181** | **334** |
| 1 | 2000 | 10 | 303 | 493 |
| 1 | 10000 | 10 | 269 | 531 |
| 3 | 5000 | 10 | 226 | 359 |
| 6 | 1000 | 5 | 286 | 504 |

- **Serial commits (concurrency 1) are slowest:** nothing overlaps.
- **More, smaller transactions also lose:** they spend more time queueing on the same alert-row locks.

**Client connections, LT-C (completion / p99, ms):**

| Connections | Completion | p99 | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 64 | 5,453 | 5,312 | fail |
| 128 | 3,112 | 3,042 | fail |
| 192 | 1,979 | 1,846 | 1 of 3 runs failed |
| 256 | 1,306 | 1,267 | pass |
| **512** (used) | **945** | **880** | pass |
| 768 | 942 | 891 | pass |
| 1,000 | 1,141 | 1,056 | pass |

- **Below ~256 connections, the client can't keep enough requests in flight** to cover the ~35 ms each one waits for its commit.
- **512–768 is the sweet spot.** Beyond that, the extra sockets cost more than they add.
- **10,000 independent single-reading senders** would bring at least this much concurrency, so 512 is a fair stand-in.

### A measurement pitfall that was found and fixed

The first version of the harness sampled server CPU with `pidusage`. On Windows 11, where `wmic` is gone, that library starts a new `powershell.exe` for every sample, ten times a second. That starved the server and PostgreSQL and inflated every result:

| Same build and settings | LT-A completion | LT-C completion (1,000 connections) |
|---|---|---|
| Sampled with `pidusage` | 0.58–2.44 s | 6.0–12.6 s |
| Sampled in-process (`loadtest/probe.mjs`) | 0.14–0.32 s | 1.1–1.3 s |

How it was tracked down:
1. **Per-step commit timings:** a trivial `BEGIN` took up to 333 ms.
2. **`pg_stat_activity` sampling:** backends were waiting on the client (`ClientRead`).
3. **Eliminations:** two other suspects were ruled out first. OS throttling of the spawned process was tested with a CPU benchmark: same speed. GC was traced: 44 ms worst pause, 33 MB heap.
4. **Comparison:** the same server, burst from outside the harness, was fast.

The harness now measures the server from the inside, over IPC, without starting any processes.

### Caveats and limits

- **The load generator shares the machine** with the server and PostgreSQL (14 logical threads on 12 hybrid cores, 15 W). On separate machines the server would have more CPU to itself.
- **Variance:** first runs after a pause are sometimes slower (e.g. LT-C run 1). The pass criteria are applied to every run, not to averages.
- **Window memory grows with reading rate × window length.** Server memory rose from 122 MB to 255 MB across this test, because each reading is held in every matching time window (up to 10 minutes). That's fine for bursts. For sustained 10k/s with 10-minute windows, samples should be pre-aggregated into fixed per-second buckets per (rule, sensor). That would make memory proportional to window seconds instead of readings.
- **A single process is a deliberate design choice:** window state has one owner (design §9). Going beyond one event loop's ~3–12k single requests/s (on this laptop) needs:
  - batching at sensor gateways (already ~5× cheaper), or
  - partitioning sensors across processes, for example a log such as Kafka partitioned by `sensorId`.

### Reproduce

```sh
pnpm loadtest                                 # all scenarios, 3 runs, rewrites the generated section above
pnpm loadtest --scenarios C --single-connections 256 --no-report
FLUSH_CONCURRENCY=1 pnpm loadtest --scenarios A,B --no-report   # server knobs pass through
LOG_LEVEL=debug LOADTEST_SERVER_LOG=server.log pnpm loadtest --scenarios A --runs 1 --no-report   # per-batch timings
```
